judgment_calls: Test scenarios are a closed, code-owned registry (`tool_test_scenarios.ts`, shared with D1.3's validator) of 3 fixed, non-sensitive CLI invocations (`--version`, `--help`, no-args) — a `tool-install` proposal selects 2 or 3 of these BY IDENTIFIER, never by prompt text. This keeps the track's no-raw-prompts invariant structural (there is no field capable of carrying prompt text at all) while still genuinely invoking the installed candidate, closing the D1.2 repair's Blocker B gap.

Each scenario's stdout/stderr is redirected into a transient, on-disk (bind-mounted, host-side-but-scratch) log purely for the SAME network/credential-signature scanning the install step already used, then discarded with the rest of the scratch directory — never returned, never logged, never persisted raw.

Forbidden-path violations are detected via pre-seeded sentinel files with a known content hash, checked for a content/hash change (or disappearance) after the run — verified by hand to work under the container's user (a permission-bit/chmod-000 approach was considered and rejected: even a non-root process that OWNS a file it wrote can still corrupt it, so hash comparison is the only reliable signal regardless of container user).

Credential ACCESS attempts (reads, not writes) are counted by how many times a sentinel's marker text appears in the captured install+invocation output — a `cat`/read prints the sentinel's content, which the run script redirects into logs this module parses for a COUNT ONLY; the raw log content itself is discarded and never returned or persisted.

Teardown correctness (`docker kill` + `docker rm -f` in a `finally`, not relying on `--rm` alone, targeting only the exact generated name) was verified BY HAND against this environment before being encoded: killing the `docker run` CLI client process (e.g. on a timeout) does NOT stop the container — `--rm` only fires on the CONTAINER's own exit, not its client's.

Install methods are a closed, explicit set (`npm install`, `pip install`, plus a TEST-ONLY `local-script` escape hatch never accepted by the production proposal validator in D1.3) — an unrecognised installMethod fails closed to `verdict: 'unknown', reason: 'unsupported_install_method'` rather than guessing at a shell invocation.

The container now runs as the `node:22-alpine` image's built-in non-root `node` user with a read-only root filesystem; the bind-mounted `/vet` scratch workspace is chmod 0o777 on the host side specifically so a non-root, non-host-uid-mapped container user can still create/modify files there regardless of which uid created the directory — verified against the real local Docker daemon by the full real-Docker suite passing unchanged with these flags applied.

The live Docker tests use `node:22-alpine` (already present locally in this environment, confirmed via `docker images` before writing any code) specifically to avoid any image-pull network dependency in the test suite; `--pull never` is also passed on every real `docker run` so a missing image fails fast and deterministically rather than the vetting infrastructure itself silently reaching the internet.

The 'network calls observed' detection is a closed set of known DNS/connection-failure error signatures (`getaddrinfo`, `Could not resolve host`, `failed to connect`, `ENETUNREACH`, `ECONNREFUSED`) parsed out of captured install+invocation output under `--network none`; a network-capable ecosystem tool not covered by one of these signatures would under-report rather than over-report — ponytail: extend the signature list if a real generator surfaces one this misses.

The test suite's scratch root is now created under `os.tmpdir()` (guaranteed to exist on every platform) rather than a hardcoded absolute path assumed to pre-exist, and is torn down only via its own tracked path in `afterAll` — never a sweep of anything else under the OS tmp directory.

SUPERSEDED-IN-PART by the 2026-08-21 repair_2 pass: verdict priority order is now forbidden-path violation → credential access attempt → (install/scenario success gate) → network calls observed → safe. Both unsafe signals are checked BEFORE the success gate, so a run that fails to install/invoke but ALSO touches a forbidden path or reads a credential sentinel is still classified `unsafe`, never `unknown` — an unsafe signal is always the strongest verdict regardless of whether the candidate otherwise 'worked'.

`evaluateCandidateSucceeded` treats `scenarioIds.length` as the exact requested-set size without re-deduplicating, relying on the fact that `vetToolInSandboxAsync`'s own `validateScenarioIds` (unchanged, upstream of any runtime call) already rejects a duplicate scenario id before `DockerSandboxRuntime.runAsync` — and therefore this function — is ever reached with one.

The pre-existing 'network call → conditional' real-Docker fixture (`network-fixture`) previously used a `packageSource` install script that called `process.exit(1)` on the network error — which, under the repair_2 success-gated contract, would now correctly reclassify to `unknown` (the install itself failed). Since this fixture's INTENT is 'a tool that attempts a network call but still works' (the scenario 'conditional' exists to describe), it was updated to also write a working candidate binary and drop the explicit `process.exit(1)`, rather than weakening the new success gate to accommodate a fixture that no longer matched what it was meant to demonstrate.

credentialAccessAttemptsCount under the new mechanism counts DISTINCT sentinels whose atime advanced (0–3), not repeat-read counts against the same sentinel — relatime-style atime coalescing on a second read of the same already-touched file within the run cannot be relied upon to advance atime again. This is sufficient because classifyVerdict only ever checks `> 0`; exact repeat-count fidelity was never part of the contract.

The old per-sentinel content-hash check was removed entirely rather than kept alongside the new existence check, because it was the direct SOURCE of a new false-positive class this pass discovered (the run script's own `sha256sum` read advancing the same atime the host observer trusts) — keeping it disabled-by-default or gated would have been a needless extra branch for a check that can no longer detect anything real once the sentinel directory is `:ro` (a successful content change is now structurally impossible).

repair_3.authorized_by: AJ (explicit, out-of-band authorization for a bounded credential-observer redesign after GPT reproduced a real-Docker acceptance/security failure post-repair_2)
repair_3.blocker: Credential ACCESS detection only ever counted a sentinel's marker text appearing in captured install/invoke stdout/stderr. A quiet read (`cat /vet/sentinel/aws_credentials >/dev/null 2>&1; exit 0`, installed via `local-script` as `quiet-reader`) left that text nowhere in any log, so `credentialAccessAttemptsCount` stayed 0 and the run reached `verdict: 'safe'` despite a real credential read having happened.
repair_3.root_cause: Detection was entirely a function of the candidate's own captured output — an untrusted channel the candidate fully controls (any redirection suppresses it). This is a class of bug, not a single missed case: the same weakness applies to any read whose output the candidate hides, regardless of tool (shell `cat`, a programmatic `fs.readFileSync`, or anything else).
repair_3.redesign: Credential-access detection is now observed independently of candidate stdout/stderr, from the HOST's own filesystem view, entirely outside the container: each sentinel file is written directly by the host (never by a script running at the candidate's own privilege) into a directory bind-mounted into the container as its OWN separate `:ro` (read-only) mount at `/vet/sentinel` — distinct from the `:rw` `/vet` workspace the candidate's install/scenario steps use. The host records each sentinel's `atime` immediately after writing it (before the container starts), and re-reads it entirely after the container exits: any advance proves a real `open()`+`read()` happened against that exact file, regardless of what the candidate did with the content. The `:ro` mount makes this tamper-resistant — verified empirically that `touch -a` (reset atime), `rm` (delete), and a programmatic `fs.unlinkSync` from inside the container all fail with `EROFS`, so a candidate that reads a sentinel and then tries to erase the evidence cannot succeed. A forbidden-path WRITE attempt (as distinct from a read) can no longer land at all under the `:ro` mount; it is instead recognised, best-effort, from the install/invoke logs' own OS-level 'Read-only file system'/'Permission denied' error text naming the sentinel path — the attempt itself is the violation. A FIFO/named-pipe blocking-handshake mechanism was investigated first and rejected after hand-verification against this environment's actual Docker Desktop (linuxkit VM, virtiofs-backed bind mounts): a container-side `ls` on the containing directory alone was observed to spuriously unblock a host-side FIFO writer with no candidate read at all — an unacceptable false-positive source specific to this bind-mount implementation. Plain regular files + `atime` do not share this problem (re-verified: `ls`/`stat` never advances a regular file's `atime`, only a real `open()`+`read()` does, verified both without Docker and through the exact hardened `docker run` flag set used in production).
repair_3.observer_failure_handling: If the host-side observer cannot write/stat its sentinel files before the run (`SandboxObserverError` from `setupCredentialSentinels`) or cannot read them back after (`SandboxObserverError` from `computeCredentialAccess`, e.g. a sentinel file has vanished), the whole run fails closed to `verdict: 'unknown'`, fixed reason `sandbox_observer_unavailable` — never inferred as "zero access".
repair_3.limitations_disclosed: This mechanism proves access to the THREE NAMED synthetic sentinel files it seeds — it is not a generic syscall-level file-access auditor (no `strace`/`ptrace`/audit framework is used or assumed available in `node:22-alpine`, and none was found necessary for this bounded fix; a broader generic auditor was explicitly out of scope per the redesign brief). It also does not attempt to enumerate every conceivable forbidden-path WRITE attempt — the log-text-based write-attempt signal is best-effort and can be defeated by a candidate that redirects that specific error text away, unlike the read-side atime signal which is structurally independent of anything the candidate controls. The `:ro` mount is what actually PREVENTS a write/delete from succeeding regardless of whether the attempt itself is detected.

repair_4.authorized_by: AJ (continuation of the same bounded D1 credential-observer correction after the prior agent account was rate-limited)
repair_4.blocker: The atime observer treated unchanged credential-sentinel atimes as zero access without first proving that this host, bind mount, and timestamp behavior could expose any atime advance. On `noatime`, unsupported propagation, or an unobservable timestamp resolution, a quiet real read could still reach `safe`.
repair_4.correction: A separate code-owned `.observer_capability_probe` is written in the same trusted host sentinel directory and nested `/vet/sentinel:ro` mount, but is excluded from the credential-sentinel registry and count. Before any candidate-controlled install or scenario command, the trusted runner reads that probe exactly once. The host then requires its deliberately-aged baseline atime to advance after container exit before it evaluates named credential sentinels; missing, malformed, unreadable, or unchanged proof throws `SandboxObserverError`, mapping to fixed `unknown` reason `sandbox_observer_unavailable`. Every probe and sentinel baseline is explicitly aged behind its preserved mtime before capture, so relatime eligibility never depends on two operations falling in different wall-clock milliseconds.
repair_4.boundary: This is positive capability proof for the same named-sentinel, nested read-only mount boundary only. It is not a generic syscall/file-access audit, and a later candidate read of the probe never creates a credential-access count.
